dislocation.

Overview
The saddle-shaped sternoclavicular joint (SCJ) consists of the articulation between the medial
clavicle and the sternum.
SCJ injuries are uncommon and range from instability (asymptomatic and symptomatic) to
dislocation, infection, and degenerative disease.
SCJ dislocations result from high-energy trauma, indirectly transmitted from the shoulder
through the clavicle or directly to the joint.
Anterior SCJ instability is far more common than posterior injuries.
Most anterior SCJ dislocations can be successfully managed nonsurgically.
The prompt diagnosis of a posterior SCJ dislocation is crucial because compression of vital
posterior structures may be life-threatening.
Epidemiology
Injuries to the SCJ are relatively rare and represent less than 3% of all traumatic joint
injuries.1,2
SCJ dislocations represent 1% of all orthopaedic dislocations.3
Anterior SCJ dislocations are much more common than posterior dislocations, likely secondary
to the robust strength of the posterior ligamentous structures.1,4

Epidemiology
Injuries to the SCJ include dislocation, instability (acute and chronic), and degenerative
disease. Traumatic SCJ injuries are relatively rare and are estimated to represent less
than 3% of all traumatic joint injuries,2 1% of all orthopaedic dislocations,3 and 0.5% to
5% of all shoulder girdle injuries.4,5 Anterior SCJ instability is much more common than
posterior instability, with a case series by Boesmueller et al5 estimating that anterior
dislocations are at least twice as common as posterior dislocations. This is likely
secondary to the robust strength of the posterior SCJ ligamentous structures, with
biomechanical studies demonstrating a 50% reduced force necessary for an anterior SCJ
dislocation compared with a posterior dislocation.1,4,6

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The SCJ is a saddle-shaped joint that joins the appendicular skeleton to the axial skeleton.
The relative incongruity between the medial clavicle and the manubrium/first rib leads to very
little bony stability.
The relatively low dislocation rate of the SCJ is secondary to the supporting soft-tissue
structures, including the intra-articular disk, capsular, interclavicular, and costoclavicular
(rhomboid) ligaments.
The medial clavicle physis is the last physis in the body to close, not closing until age 23 to 25
years.7
Posterior SCJ dislocations in patients younger than 25 years warrant careful consideration
because these injuries often are fracture-dislocations of the medial clavicle physis.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The SCJ consists of the articulation between the medial clavicle and the shallow socket
formed by the first costal cartilage and the manubrium. The SCJ is a saddle-shaped joint
with limited inherent bony stability. The relatively low dislocation rate of the SCJ is
secondary to the supporting soft-tissue structures, including the intra-articular disk,
capsular, interclavicular, and costoclavicular (rhomboid) ligaments. The joint capsule
extends from the manubrium laterally to the clavicular epiphysis and provides restraint
to translation in the axial plane. The posterior capsule is much more robust than the
anterior capsule and serves as the primary stabilizer to anterior-posterior translation of
the SCJ. The interclavicular ligament courses from the superomedial portion of each
clavicle and also reinforces the SCJ.8 The costoclavicular ligament is the strongest of the
SCJ ligamentous structures.9 It is an extracapsular ligament that extends from the
inferomedial clavicle to the first rib/costal cartilage.8 The blood supply to the SCJ is
comprised of articular branches of the suprascapular and internal thoracic arteries.
Innervation is supplied by the medial suprascapular nerve and the nerve to the
subclavius muscle (Figure 1; Resources 1 and 2).

18 to 20 years and does not fully close until age 23 to 25 years.7 Posterior dislocations in
this age group often represent fracture-dislocations of the medial clavicular physis.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
SCJ dislocations result from high-energy trauma transmitted from the shoulder through the
clavicle or directly to the joint.
Common mechanisms of injury include motor vehicle collisions, falls from a height, and
contact athletics (Resource 3).
If the SCJ supporting ligamentous structures fail to heal postinjury, joint instability or static
subluxation may result in persistent pain and dysfunction.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
SCJ dislocations result from high-energy trauma transmitted from the shoulder through
the clavicle or directly to the joint (Figure 2). A direct anterior-to-posterior force to the
SCJ may result in a posterior dislocation because the medial clavicle is pushed behind
the sternum. More often, injury occurs after indirect force, causing anterolateral or
posterolateral compression to the shoulder.1 Posterior instability may occur if a lateral
compressive force is applied to the shoulder as it rolls forward. An anterior dislocation
occurs with a backward motion of the shoulder under lateral compression.1 Frequent
mechanisms of injury include motor vehicle collisions, falls from a height, and contact
athletics. Motor vehicle collisions and sports injuries are most common, accounting for
more than 80% of all dislocations.6 Omer10 reviewed 82 SCJ dislocations managed at 14
military hospitals and found that 47% resulted from motor vehicle collisions and 31%
resulted from athletic injuries.

Risk Factors
Risk factors for atraumatic SCJ instability include generalized ligamentous laxity conditions,
such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Associated Injuries
Concomitant injuries are common in patients with a traumatic dislocation of the SCJ given the
frequent high-energy mechanism of injury.
Anterior dislocations are unlikely to lead to direct injury to other thoracic structures.
The prompt diagnosis of a posterior SCJ dislocation is crucial because compression of
posterior vital structures may be life-threatening.


Associated Injuries
Concomitant injuries are common in patients with a traumatic dislocation of the SCJ
given the frequent high-energy mechanism of injury and include rib fractures,
pneumothoraxes, long bone fractures, facial fractures, and spinal column injuries. In
patients with a SCJ dislocation, the displaced clavicle may lead to injury or compression
of nearby vital structures. Anterior dislocations are unlikely to lead to direct injury to
other thoracic structures given the subcutaneous location of the SCJ. Posterior SCJ
dislocations warrant prompt diagnosis because compression/injury to posterior
neurovascular or pulmonary structures may be life-threatening.
Injury Classification
Injuries to the SCJ can be classified according to the severity of the injury (sprain, subluxation,
or dislocation), direction of the injury (anterior or posterior), chronicity of the injury (acute,
chronic, persistent, congenital), or age of the patient (skeletally immature or skeletally mature).
Injury Severity
SCJ injuries can be described based on the severity of soft-tissue injury according to the Allman
classification system.11
Grade I: partial ligamentous and capsular disruption (mild sprain)
Grade II: injury to the intra-articular disk and joint capsule; however, the costoclavicular
ligament remains intact (subluxation)
Grade III: complete disruption of the ligamentous complex (dislocation)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
SCJ injuries can be easily missed in polytrauma patients; therefore, a high clinical suspicion is
key.
Anterior subluxation/dislocation injuries may lead to a prominence of the medial clavicle,
whereas posterior instability may result in a visible defect or palpable step-off in the area of

the SCJ.
Compression of the mediastinal structures occurs in as many as 25% of patients with a
posterior dislocation of the SCJ and must be promptly identified.
Traumatic Subluxation

Traumatic Subluxation
With grade I injuries of the SCJ, patients report a pop or click after trauma or direct
contact immediately followed by pain over the anterior chest and swelling in the area of
the SCJ. Patients with a grade II injury or subluxation event will describe pain with
movement of the ipsilateral upper extremity and soft-tissue swelling. In patients with
recurrent instability or subluxation, the medial clavicle may subluxate with shoulder
extension or overhead activity but reduce spontaneously. This often can be reproduced
at will by the patient in chronic cases. On physical examination, the SCJ may be tender to
palpation and swollen. Active range of motion of the ipsilateral upper extremity
reproduces pain. Anterior subluxation may be obvious via direct inspection; however,
posterior subluxation may be more subtle. Anterior injuries often exhibit some dynamic
subluxation of the medial clavicle, whereas posterior injuries are more static in nature.
Anterior Dislocations

Anterior Dislocations
Patients with an anterior SCJ dislocation present with a painful lump adjacent to the
manubrium. On physical examination, the ipsilateral shoulder may appear shortened
compared with the contralateral limb, with the medial end of the clavicle visibly
prominent. In patients with a severe dislocation, the medial clavicle may be identified on
the anterior surface of the sternum. Anterior dislocations may be freely mobile or fixed.
These may be quite painful, with patients holding the affected extremity in adduction to
prevent scapulothoracic and glenohumeral motion. Injury to the posteriorly based
thoracic structures, although possible, is unlikely. If a patient is younger than 25 years, a

medial clavicle physeal injury should be considered; however, physeal fractures are
more common in patients with a posterior injury.
Posterior Dislocations

Posterior Dislocations
With posterior SCJ dislocations, patients may present with a palpable defect or step-off
at the injured SCJ. The medial clavicle is displaced posteriorly; however, this often is
difficult to appreciate visually because of soft-tissue swelling. A meta-analysis of
posterior SCJ dislocations demonstrated that 47% of patients had other symptoms in
addition to pain, swelling, and decreased motion.12 Because of the relatively close
proximity of major vessels, the esophagus, the trachea, and the brachial plexus, patients
with a posterior SCJ dislocation may exhibit myriad symptoms, including ipsilateral upper
extremity venous congestion or cyanosis, stridor, hoarseness, cough, shortness of
breath, dysphagia, or a choking sensation. The symptoms often are positional, with
patients in the supine position exhibiting more symptoms. A thorough neurologic
examination may reveal ipsilateral upper-extremity paresthesias or weakness secondary
to compression of the brachial plexus. If any of the symptoms are identified, urgent
reduction of the posterior SCJ dislocation is necessary. SCJ injuries may be easily missed
in polytrauma patients; therefore, a high clinical suspicion is key. If the patient is
sedated, altered, obtunded, or intubated, an axial CT scan should be thoroughly
scrutinized.
Neurovascular Examination
Because of the relatively close proximity of major vessels and the brachial plexus, patients with
a posterior SCJ dislocation may exhibit myriad symptoms, including ipsilateral upper extremity
venous congestion, cyanosis, or neurologic dysfunction.
Compression of mediastinal structures occurs in as many as 25% of patients with a posterior
dislocation of the SCJ.1


Neurovascular Examination
Compression of mediastinal structures occurs in as many as 25% of patients with a
posterior dislocation of the SCJ.1 Neurovascular symptoms, such as venous
congestion/cyanosis of the upper extremity from injury/compression of the subclavian
vessels or ipsilateral paresthesias from compression of the nearby brachial plexus, may
occur. If compression or injury to the posterior mediastinal structures is identified,
urgent reduction is necessary. In patients with a posterior SCJ dislocation who do not
have neurovascular symptoms, serial examinations should be performed because
compression may develop over time secondary to soft-tissue swelling or hematoma
formation.
Imaging Studies
SCJ injuries frequently are missed during the initial evaluation because displacement of the
medial clavicle is difficult to assess via conventional plain radiographs.
CT, MRI, and ultrasonography are useful imaging modalities to diagnose SCJ pathology.
Radiography
An AP radiograph of the chest and a serendipity radiograph of sternoclavicular joints are
recommended.
AP View

AP View
A routine AP radiograph of the chest often is the first imaging study obtained in patients
with a SCJ injury, especially in those who sustain high-energy trauma. An AP chest
radiograph also should be obtained if any suspicion for a posterior dislocation of the SCJ
exists to evaluate for associated injury, including pneumomediastinum or
pneumothorax. Dislocation of the acromioclavicular joint may be identified on a chest
radiograph if the SCJ is displaced compared with the contralateral side in assessing the

relative craniocaudal position of the medial clavicle. Anterior subluxation or dislocation
of the SCJ will lead to the clavicle being superiorly displaced on AP chest radiographs.
Posterior injuries are considerably more difficult to assess on chest radiographs.
Serendipity View

Serendipity View
The serendipity view was first described by Rockwood in 1975.2 A serendipity view is an
oblique radiograph of the SCJ obtained by positioning the patient supine with the x-ray
beam directed at the sternum and angled 40° cephalad (Figure 3). A serendipity
radiograph is helpful because it allows for comparison of the injured and uninjured SCJs
in the same plane and can help determine superior or inferior displacement of the
medial clavicle.1 An anteriorly subluxated or dislocated clavicle will appear superior on a
serendipity radiograph. A posteriorly subluxated or dislocated clavicle will appear
inferior on a serendipity radiograph.

Computed Tomography
A CT scan of the chest is recommended for definitive diagnosis of SCJ subluxation or
dislocation.
A CT angiogram is recommended for posterior subluxation or dislocation to rule out vascular
injury.

Computed Tomography
Because plain radiographs of the SCJ often are difficult to obtain and interpret, an axial
CT scan is the best imaging study to fully evaluate the SCJ (Figure 4). In patients with a
posterior dislocation, CT angiography also should be performed if any vascular injury is
suspected or present. Patients with chronic or delayed presentation of posterior SCJ
instability also should undergo CT angiography. A CT scan also should be obtained after
attempted closed reduction to confirm appropriate joint alignment.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may be considered in skeletally immature patients to decrease radiation exposure and
evaluate for physeal fractures versus dislocation.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is a useful imaging modality to evaluate the soft-tissue structures about the SCJ,
including the joint capsule, costoclavicular ligament, posterior neurovascular structures,
trachea, and esophagus. In pediatric patients with a SCJ injury, MRI may be preferred
over CT given the lack of radiation exposure. In pediatric and adolescent patients, MRI
also can be performed to differentiate an SCJ dislocation from a physeal injury.
Compared with CT, MRI provides information on the bone marrow, the cartilage,

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography can be used to evaluate SCJ stability.

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is a useful imaging modality and that allows for a dynamic view of the
SCJ. Previous research demonstrated that ultrasonography is more accurate than
conventional radiographs with regard to diagnose SCJ dislocations.13 Ultrasonography is
particularly useful in the emergency room because it allows for rapid diagnosis of
posterior dislocations. The role of ultrasonography also is being expanded in the setting
of athletic event coverage, with portable units allowing for easy use in the athletic
training room or on the sideline.

Management
In patients with a SCJ traumatic injury, the acuity of injury, the direction of displacement,
neurovascular compromise, and symptom severity should be considered in formulating a

14/26

treatment strategy.
Most injuries are managed nonsurgically because of generally favorable results and the risk for
substantial complications with surgical management.
SCJ injuries are rare; therefore, few orthopaedic surgeons are comfortable and/or have
experience with open reduction and stabilization techniques (Resource 4).
Nonsurgical Management
Grade I and grade II SCJ sprains and subluxations should be managed nonsurgically.
Anterior SCJ dislocations typically are managed nonsurgically via closed reduction.
Posterior dislocations of the SCJ are considered true orthopaedic emergencies because of
possible compromise of vital structures posterior to the mediastinum.
Patients with an acute traumatic posterior dislocation without identified mediastinal injury
should be treated via closed reduction under a general anesthetic agent, with conversion to
open reduction and stabilization if irreducible or inherently unstable.
Sprain/Subluxation
Grade I and grade II injuries typically are managed via immobilization.

Sprain/Subluxation
Grade I and grade II SCJ injuries should be managed nonsurgically, with patients
responding well to a brief period of immobilization in a sling, ice, pain control, and
physical therapy.14 Patients with a grade I injury generally undergo immobilization for 1
to 3 weeks, followed by gentle return to activity under the guidance of a physical
therapist. Patients should avoid contact activity and be allowed to return to normal
activities, including sports activity, in 4 to 6 weeks after shoulder range of motion is pain-
free and full strength has returned.15 In patients with a grade II subluxation injury, joint
reduction should be attempted. The patient then undergoes immobilization in a sling for
4 to 6 weeks. This allows for the soft-tissue stabilizers of the SCJ to scar and heal.
Physical therapy focusing on shoulder range of motion with a gradual strengthening
program can be initiated after 3 to 4 weeks. Return to full activity can occur after 6 to 8
weeks. Patients with a subluxation injury should be counseled about the possibility of

asymmetry at the SCJ or persistent bony prominence; however, this cosmetic deformity
generally is well tolerated.
Anterior Dislocation
Anterior SCJ dislocations usually are managed via reduction and immobilization.
Surgical treatment usually is reserved for patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails,
patients with an irreducible dislocation, and patients with a grossly displaced injury.

Anterior Dislocation
Anterior SCJ dislocations typically are managed nonsurgically via closed reduction
(Figure 5). Nonsurgical treatment is favored in patients with these injuries because
anterior dislocations are considered to result in little long-term functional effects.16
Timely closed reduction is recommended for acute anterior instability because such
injury is inherently unstable.17 Glass at al18 performed a systematic review of 241 SCJ
injuries and reported that acute anterior dislocations initially managed via closed
reduction resulted in superior functional outcomes than those managed via open
reduction. Attempted closed reduction of anterior dislocations should be performed
with the patient under conscious sedation or general anesthesia. To perform closed
reduction, the patient is placed in the supine position with a towel roll between the
scapulae. The arm is positioned in 90° of abduction, and traction is applied. A posterior-
directed force is applied to the medial clavicle. After successful reduction, the extremity
should be placed in a sling for at least 6 weeks to decrease the risk of recurrent
instability; however, patients should be informed of the high risk of recurrent anterior
dislocation with nonsurgical management.2 Recurrent anterior instability rates after
closed reduction are estimated to be between 21% and 100%.17 Despite the risk of
recurrent instability, nonsurgical management is effective, with good or excellent results
achieved in 70% of patients treated nonsurgically.16

in patients with a traumatic displacement and grossly displaced dislocation. In patients
with chronic symptomatic anterior SCJ instability, open reduction and stabilization can
be performed.19 Surgical stabilization involves open reduction and soft-tissue
reconstruction of damaged ligamentous stabilizers (Figure 6).

management of anterior dislocation or instability. A, Drill holes are created on the
anterior manubrium and the clavicle approximately 15 to 20 mm from the joint line.

Posterior Dislocation

Posterior SCJ subluxations and dislocations are orthopaedic emergencies requiring a complete
workup.
Urgent reduction in the operating room is recommended.

Posterior Dislocation
Posterior dislocations of the SCJ are considered true orthopaedic emergencies because
of possible compromise of the vital structures posterior to the mediastinum.20 If a
posterior SCJ dislocation is identified or suspected, the patient must be carefully
evaluated to rule out concomitant compression/injury to the esophagus, brachial plexus,
lungs, trachea, and great vessels. Compression of mediastinal structures occurs in as
many as 25% of patients with a posterior dislocation of the SCJ and must promptly be
identified.1 CT angiography is indicated in patients in whom any suspicion of vascular
injury exists. Patients with an acute traumatic posterior dislocation who do not have a
mediastinal injury should be treated via closed reduction under a general anesthetic
agent.2 Ideally, closed reduction of posterior dislocations should only be attempted in a
controlled environment under general anesthesia because reduction of the medial
clavicle may damage or relieve tamponade of great vessels, leading to acute life-
threatening hemodynamic instability. A notable exception is if evidence of vascular or
airway compromise is noted, which warrants emergent reduction. Vascular or thoracic
surgeons should be on standby during closed or open reduction to address any potential
injury to the posterior mediastinal structures. If a patient decompensates after
reduction, the clavicle should be re-displaced posteriorly to attempt tamponade of the
source. Thoracic or vascular surgery assistance is necessary for this reason. If a
posteriorly dislocated clavicle is irreducible or reduction cannot be maintained, then
open reduction and stabilization can be performed acutely or under subsequent
anesthesia.21,22
The abduction traction technique is a well-described method for closed reduction of
posterior injuries.2 In this technique, the patient is placed in the supine position with the
affected shoulder near the end of the table. A small towel bump is placed between the
scapulae. The arm is abducted, and gentle traction is applied while countertraction is
provided by an assistant stabilizing the patient on the table. Traction on the arm in the

abducted position is slowly increased as the arm is brought into extension. This results
in an anteriorly directed force transmitted to the clavicle, reducing the medial clavicle.
The clavicle typically reduces with an audible pop and usually is stable. If traction and
shoulder extension is unsuccessful, the diaphysis of the clavicle can be manually pulled
anteriorly in patients with a favorable body habitus. Alternatively, under sterile
conditions, a towel clip or pointed reduction clamp can be used to percutaneously grasp
the clavicle and bring it anteriorly. Prompt attempts at reduction are more successful,
with a meta-analysis on posterior SCJ dislocations reporting a 55.8% success rate if
reduction is performed within 48 hours postinjury and a 30.8% success rate if reduction
is delayed more than 48 hours postinjury.12 If not reduced, severe complications,
including pneumothorax, esophageal compression, brachial plexus injury, and thoracic
outlet syndrome, have been reported in approximately 30% of patients with traumatic
injuries, with mortality rates reaching 3% to 4%.6 After closed reduction, CT or
intraoperative O-arm evaluation should be performed to evaluate the SCJ reduction and
the posterior mediastinal structures.23 Dissimilar from anterior dislocations, most
posterior injuries are stable after redution.18 After confirmation of reduction, patients
may undergo immobilization in a sling for 4 to 6 weeks, followed by initiation of physical
therapy and gradual return to full activity after 6 to 8 weeks if strength and range of
motion are restored. Surgical management of posterior SCJ dislocations is indicated in
patients in whom closed reduction is unsuccessful, patients with recurrent posterior
instability, and patients with evidence of associated major thoracic structure injury.
Medial Clavicle Physeal Injuries
Most posterior SCJ injuries in skeletally immature patients are physeal fractures.
Posteriorly displaced physeal fractures should be urgently reduced in a manner
similar to that for posterior dislocations.
Surgical reduction and internal fixation can be performed in patients with a SCJ injury
in whom reduction cannot be maintained.

SCJ dislocations in patients younger than 25 years frequently are physeal fractures
rather than true dislocations. Minimally displaced anterior physeal injuries typically are
managed nonsurgically. Similar to most clavicle fractures, physeal injuries typically heal
without complications. Bone remodeling usually minimizes cosmetic deformity. Closed
reduction should be performed in patients with a displaced anterior physeal injury. The
displaced clavicle is reduced to the medial clavicle epiphysis, which remains with the
sternum. Chronic anterior physeal injuries should be managed symptomatically.
Nonsurgical management of posterior SCJ physeal fractures has been reported but with
the risk of complications, such as pneumothorax24 and thoracic outlet syndrome
secondary to callus formation.25 Acute posterior injuries are managed via closed
reduction under a general anesthetic agent, with reported success rates ranging from
30% to 50%.12,26 As time to reduction is delayed, difficulty of reduction (closed or open)
drastically increases. Open reduction is indicated in patients with an irreducible injuries,
an injury with persistent instability, associated major thoracic injury, or a subacute
injury.22 In these patients, the epiphysis remains stable and located with the manubrium
and the medial clavicle dislocates posteriorly. Suture repair of grossly unstable posterior
physeal fractures can be performed.22 Sutures are passed through metaphyseal bone
drill hole tunnels lateral to the fracture, with the sutures exiting the fracture site. Heavy
suture is then passed through the epiphyseal fragment, holding the clavicle in reduction
(Figure 7).
